sections.h2: Which Marion County offices handle your bill?
sections.html:
One office values, one bills, and one keeps the records: the appraiser, the tax collector and the clerk of court. All three work out of the Ocala area, and each has its own website.

  • Marion County Property Appraiser: parcel and sales search, a property tax estimator, homestead e-filing, TPP return e-filing, a page of important dates and information on the TRIM notice and the Value Adjustment Board. The office lists its address as 501 SE 25th Avenue, Ocala, with walk-ins welcome or appointments available.
  • Marion County Tax Collector: pay taxes online, search the tax roll, apply for a tax deed online, buy county-held certificates, and read about installment plans, deferred taxes and delinquent taxes. The main office is at the McPherson Complex, 503 SE 25th Avenue, Ocala, and the office runs eight locations across the county.
  • Marion County Clerk of Court and Comptroller: the county recorder, the keeper of Official Records, and the office that handles tax deed sales and the Value Adjustment Board.

Pick the right door before you call: value and exemptions belong to the appraiser, and amounts owed belong to the collector.

sections.h2: When are Marion County property taxes due?
sections.html:
The tax collector's payment page lists November 1 as the due date and April 1 as the delinquency date for Marion County taxes and assessments. Florida allows a discount for early payment starting in November.

Early payment discounts on the Marion County Tax Collector's payment page
Month paidDiscount
November4%
December3%
January2%
February1%
MarchGross amount, no discount

On or after April 1 the amount you owe depends on the day the collector receives your payment, not the postmark. The office also notes that taxes are payable even if a bill never arrives, and that a mortgage company paying from escrow may request the bill and the owner then gets an informational copy. The collector's notice for 2026 states that the real estate, tangible personal property and railroad rolls opened for collection.

sections.h2: What can Marion County homeowners do about the bill?
sections.html:
Several options exist before a bill turns delinquent. The collector's property tax menu lists an installment plan and deferred taxes, and the state describes the rules behind both.

  • Installment plan: section 197.222 lets owners prepay and pay in installments, with May 1 as the application deadline.
  • Homestead deferral: Form DR-570 goes to the tax collector by March 31. Deferral covers the portion above 5 percent of last year's household income, and a permanent resident aged 65 or older may defer the part above 3 percent.
  • Partial payments: before the delinquency date these are at the tax collector's discretion under section 197.374.
  • Escrow: a lender holding escrow can request your bill, so check with your servicer before paying twice.

Check with the collector on which of these still fit a parcel headed to sale, since a plan tied to the current owner may not carry to a buyer.

sections.h2: What tools does the Marion County appraiser offer owners?
sections.html:
The appraiser's site lists a property tax estimator, a mortgage estimate letter request, a mailing address change form and a homestead e-file page. It also lists a form for reporting property damage and a confidential form for reporting suspected homestead fraud.

Owners who run a business or rent out a property can file a tangible personal property return electronically and request an extension. The office also posts frequently asked questions, a property taxpayer's bill of rights, reports, digital data requests and a code list. These are the first stops for an owner who wants to understand a bill before a sale.

  • Estimator: a way to model taxes for a parcel before you commit to a price.
  • Mortgage estimate letter: a document lenders and buyers ask about.
  • Address change: keeps the TRIM notice and bill reaching you after you move.

Walk-ins are welcome at the Ocala office, and appointments can be booked ahead through the website.

sections.h2: How does Marion County value homes for tax?
sections.html:
Ownership and condition on January 1 set each year's value. Exemption and classification paperwork goes in by March 1, and business personal property returns follow on April 1.

Homestead removes up to $50,000 from taxable value, with school taxes touched only by the first $25,000. The appraiser's e-file page handles the application, which must show the home was your permanent residence on January 1.

After the first year, a state cap slows increases on a homestead's assessed value, and the state's chart shows 2.7% for 2026. Other property has a separate 10 percent ceiling. A sale or other change of ownership resets the parcel to market-based value the next January, with exceptions for spouses and some transfers at death.

The TRIM notice arrives in August. Petitions to the Value Adjustment Board run through the clerk, and the clerk's office announced in July 2026 that those petitions can be e-filed.

sections.h2: What else is on a Marion County tax bill?
sections.html:
The collector's property tax menu separates ad valorem taxes from non-ad valorem assessments, and its payment page speaks of taxes and assessments together. A bill can therefore carry more than the county's general levy. The menu also offers a tax bill explanation and a page of current tax payment methods.

Questions split into two lists, one for current tax and one for delinquent tax. The office phone is (352) 368-8200, and its website lists eight county locations with lobby cameras so you can check the line before you leave home.

  • Pay online: search the tax roll by owner or parcel and pay from the same page.
  • Deferred taxes: a menu page covers the homestead deferral rules.
  • Tax certificates and deed sales: the collector's page and the clerk's page both cover these.

Read the explanation page before assuming a line item is wrong, then bring any real error to the right office.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Marion County taxes?
sections.html:
Delinquency starts April 1, and the state says certificates are sold on all unpaid items by June 1. A certificate buyer pays the bill and earns interest, but cannot press the owner for payment for two years.

The collector's menu points owners to later steps as well: an online tax deed application, online purchase of county-held certificates, and a page on delinquent taxes. The clerk lists tax deed sales and lands available for taxes among its departments. A homestead parcel carries a higher opening bid at a deed sale.

Clear a certificate early, since the amount only grows.

sections.h2: Can a Marion County house with tax owed still sell?
sections.html:
Yes. Begin with the collector's exact balance. The title company can take it out of the money the buyer brings to the table, so a sale does not need a clean tax record first.

The state's deed stamp rate is 70 cents for each $100 of price, and the clerk takes it at recording. The buyer's first bill can also come in higher than yours, because the seller's cap ends with the sale.

For an inherited house, or one behind by several years, a written payoff should come before any offer is accepted. The clerk's Property Alert Service sends a message when paperwork hits the records under your parcel or name.

faqs.q: Who sends the Marion County property tax bill?
faqs.a: The Marion County Tax Collector sends and collects the bill. The property appraiser sets the value and mails the TRIM notice in August.

faqs.q: When do Marion County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: April 1. After that date the amount due depends on when the collector receives your payment, and the postmark does not count.

faqs.q: What early payment discount does Marion County give?
faqs.a: The collector lists 4% for November, 3% for December, 2% for January and 1% for February. March payments pay the gross amount.

faqs.q: Can I apply for homestead exemption in Marion County after March 1?
faqs.a: The state deadline is March 1, with Form DR-501 going to the appraiser. Ask the appraiser's office what, if anything, is available after that date.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay all back taxes before selling in Marion County?
faqs.a: No. A balance can be paid through closing. Ask for a written payoff and find out whether a certificate exists.
